title: Quantum Co-Design of Inhomogeneous Many-Body Neutrino Fast Flavor Transformation
authors: Zoha Laraib, Sherwood Richers, Alessandro Baroni, Kathleen Hamilton, In-Saeng Suh
abstract: Dense-neutrino flavor evolution is a quantum many-body problem whose fully correlated treatment becomes rapidly more expensive with increasing particle number and spatial structure. We develop a \texttt{QCNO} quantum simulation code that maps a inhomogeneous forward-scattering neutrino Hamiltonian with advection and finite-range interactions to TEBD2 product-formula quantum circuits, and connects ideal many-body simulation, backend-aware execution, and fault-tolerant resource estimation within the same physical model. We reproduce the exact many-body evolution of the suppressed mean-field-like transverse fast flavor instability through $N=30$ and show that even a single open-boundary interaction generates Rënyi entanglement and non-stabilizer magic, although noisy backends still produce polarization RMSEs of order $0.1$--$0.3$. The restricted active interaction graph of this problem allows us to estimate the circuit depth and $T$ gate cost through $N=50$ for both NISQ and fault-tolerant approaches. The measured TEBD2 error in our fiducial ideal simulation of order $10^{-3}$ motivates a synthesis tolerance $\varepsilon_{\rm syn}\sim10^{-7}$, corresponding to about $70$ $T$ gates per $R_Z$ rotation. The generated circuit contains $1.4\times10^4$ $T$ gates per qubit for open boundaries (twice that for closed boundaries), requiring an application-level logical-$T$ error target of order $10^{-7}$ for early fault-tolerant architectures.
summary: This work introduces QCNO, a quantum simulation code designed to tackle the complex, many-body problem of neutrino flavor transformation in dense astrophysical environments. By mapping the Hamiltonian to quantum circuits, the authors simulate the system's evolution and quantify the computational resources—including required logical error rates—needed to achieve accurate results. This establishes a critical co-design pathway between advanced quantum algorithms and cutting-edge particle astrophysics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of simulating dense-neutrino flavor evolution, a quantum many-body problem, which becomes computationally prohibitive due to increasing particle number and spatial inhomogeneity.
main_result: They developed the QCNO code, successfully simulating the many-body evolution for N=30 and estimating resource requirements up to N=50, while quantifying the necessary error tolerance for fault-tolerant execution.
method: The core method involves mapping the inhomogeneous neutrino Hamiltonian to TEBD2 product-formula quantum circuits, enabling simulation via Trotter time-slicing on quantum hardware architectures.
model_or_system: The system is neutrino flavor evolution in dense, inhomogeneous fields, modeled by an inhomogeneous forward-scattering Hamiltonian incorporating advection and finite-range interactions. The simulation uses a two-flavor approximation mapped to qubits.
key_observables: Rényi entanglement, polarization RMSEs, circuit depth, and T gate cost.
important_parameters: System size N (up to 50), required synthesis tolerance $\varepsilon_{\text{syn}} \sim 10^{-7}$, and the number of qubits.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mapping the physical problem to quantum circuits and estimating resource costs for both NISQ and fault-tolerant regimes.
paper_structure: The paper details the development of the QCNO code, showing the mapping of the Hamiltonian to TEBD2 circuits, demonstrating the simulation of flavor instabilities, and finally estimating the resource scaling for fault-tolerant computation.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, application-driven framework for quantum simulation, directly linking a complex astrophysical many-body problem to the required gate counts and error correction overheads for near-term and fault-tolerant quantum computers.
